aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner because it more accurately preserves the Bellman-Ford graph topology, directed edge geometry, weight-label placement, and visual resemblance to the reference, while Figure 2 has less faithful center-to-center edge paths, awkward arrow/label placement, and more clutter around crossings. concept.rationale: Figure 2 teaches the core accuracy/precision distinctions more correctly: W is tight at the bullseye, X is a tight cluster clearly outside the lower-right target rings, and Z has two near-target and two far-off shots, matching the intended high/low accuracy and precision contrasts (L00009, L00012). aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 wins overall because it much more fully implements the intended interactions—panel selection, overlay mode, draggable/addable shots, and recalculated statistics—and it more clearly communicates the intended accuracy/precision cases, especially X entirely outside the rings and Z as inconsistent individual misses. Figure 1 is visually more faithful to the static textbook layout, with cleaner four-panel target geometry and more original-looking shot dots, but relative to Figure 2 it lacks the main interactive behaviors and has weaker conceptual treatment of some cases; Figure 2’s main drawbacks are its extra invented drag annotation, star-like markers, and somewhat less faithful panel geometry.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook geometry because it preserves the multi-part spatial layout: separate s and three p orbitals, a hybridization arrow, four individual sp³ hybrid orbitals, and a final combined tetrahedral arrangement in an orthographic/isometric view. Figure 2 has reasonably correct orbital primitives and tetrahedral directions, but it collapses the figure into a single central axes system with superimposed orbitals and a phase toggle, omitting the separate-panel arrangement, arrows, repeated axes, and final diagram structure; it also uses a perspective view that is less like a textbook schematic.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s checkbox handlers actually update the orbital contribution state, dim the corresponding atomic orbital, clear and redraw the derived hybrid/combined arrangement, and handle edge cases such as only s, only p orbitals, sp, sp2, sp3, and empty states without stale geometry. Figure 2’s controls mostly toggle visibility between two prebuilt modes; in the hybridized mode the same checkboxes hide individual hybrid lobes rather than removing s/px/py/pz contributions, so the advertised atomic-contribution interaction is not recomputed and becomes conceptually misleading.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the textbook figure because it reproduces the overall multi-part composition: separate s and p orbitals on the left, a hybridization arrow, individual sp3 hybrids, and a tetrahedral arrangement at the bottom. Figure 2 only shows the atomic orbitals superimposed on one set of axes, omitting the diagrammatic layout, hybridization progression, and tetrahedral product visible in the reference screenshot, so it reads as a different visualization rather than the same figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes most of the original figure's key labels and annotations, such as s, px, py, pz, Hybridization, sp3, and Gives a tetrahedral arrangement, whereas Figure 2 lacks essentially all of the textbook diagram labels and instead shows unrelated UI text. Figure 1's labels are small and somewhat cluttered, especially around the final tetrahedral arrangement, but Figure 2 is far worse because the actual diagram is largely unlabeled and the sidebar labels are not appropriate replacements for the original annotations.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more concept-accurate because it represents the required progression from separate pre-hybridization s, px, py, and pz orbitals to four equivalent sp3 hybrids and then to a combined tetrahedral arrangement, matching the stated one-s-plus-three-p mixing and four identical hybrids pointing to tetrahedron corners (L00010-L00012, L00018-L00019). Figure 2 also separates the content into switchable phases rather than showing the authored stepwise transformation with arrows, while Figure 1 more faithfully encodes the conceptual relationship among the stages (L00014, L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is clearly stronger because it preserves the textbook-like progression from separate s and p orbitals through hybridization to four sp³ hybrids and a final tetrahedral arrangement, with relevant labels and arrows. Figure 2 has some correct orbital primitives and tetrahedral directions, but it collapses the content into a single interactive view, omits most diagram labels and staged structure, and its controls misleadingly toggle hybrid lobes rather than recomputing atomic-orbital contributions.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the trigonal-bipyramidal PCl5 geometry with five correctly placed vertices at equal axial/equatorial distances, full split-color bonds, a matching dashed bipyramid outline, and more chemically plausible tapered hybrid-orbital lobes extending from the center toward each vertex. Figure 2 also has the correct five-direction trigonal-bipyramidal layout, but its orbital lobes are simple elongated ellipsoids rather than tapered hybrid orbitals, its atoms/bonds are proportionally smaller and less faithful to the stated textbook-style primitives, and its more face-on orthographic setup makes the 3D depth relationships less explicit than Figure 1.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the advertised cross-view interaction more directly: clicking a visible sp³d lobe switches to the molecular model and highlights the corresponding bond, while the radio toggle cleanly changes between the two representations. Figure 1’s view buttons work and its lobe click stores/highlights the matching direction, but it leaves the user in the orbital view so the corresponding molecular bond is hidden until the user manually switches views, making the advertised click-to-highlight-in-panel-a interaction less correct. Both figures have some risk from registered hidden objects still being raycastable, but Figure 2’s intended handlers better match the requested interaction overall.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful overall because its ball-and-stick model matches the reference panel (a) orientation: axial atoms are vertical, one equatorial atom extends to the right, and the other two are on the left. Figure 1 has similar colors and geometry, but it appears horizontally mirrored relative to the reference, with the single equatorial atom on the left and the pair on the right, making the composition less immediately recognizable as the same view.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 is better because it at least includes the original panel identifiers '(a)' and '(b)' in the visible labels, whereas Figure 2 omits those entirely and replaces them with invented UI text such as a title and explanatory instructions. Both figures fail to show the key in-diagram sp³d labels from the reference in the rendered view, but Figure 2 has more non-original annotation clutter and less direct correspondence to the textbook labeling.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly place five P–Cl directions in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement with two axial and three equatorial positions, matching the required PCl5 molecular geometry (L00010, L00018). Both also label five sp3d orbitals in the same trigonal-bipyramidal directions and omit small back-lobes as requested (L00007, L00012, L00018). Figure 2 is slightly more conceptually accurate because its orbital lobes are tangent to the nucleus and extend outward along each bonding direction, whereas Figure 1’s custom tapered lobe is oriented so the narrow end points toward the vertex and the broader end lies nearer the nucleus, making the “large lobe pointing at a vertex” less truthful (L00007, L00018). Figure 1 otherwise represents the bonding geometry well, but its orbital shape is more misleading than Figure 2’s simpler elongated lobes.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it more faithfully matches the rendered reference orientation and implements the intended click/toggle interaction more directly, while Figure 1 requires an extra manual view switch after a lobe click and appears mirrored relative to the reference. Figure 1 has advantages in source-level geometric construction and preserves the original panel labels better, but its tapered orbital lobes are conceptually less accurate and its labeling advantage does not outweigh Figure 2’s better visual faithfulness and interaction behavior.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the likely textbook geometry: it uses the correct 4x6 input and output grids, a 3x3 kernel, consistent skewed lattice directions, parallelogram weight cells, and a front-on orthographic view that reproduces the printed 2D convolution diagram layout. Figure 2 has the right element counts, but it converts the diagram into an isometric horizontal-plane scene with circular cells foreshortened as tilted disks and a more generic 30/30 projection, making the proportions, slopes, and initial spatial layout less faithful; it also initializes the active patch at a padded corner rather than the more central placement represented in Figure 1.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements substantially more of the requested controls correctly: play/prev/next step through valid kernel positions, clicking an output cell updates the corresponding input patch and status equation with the element-wise products, and the stride slider recomputes valid positions and marks skipped output cells. Figure 1’s sliders and animation do update the highlighted patch and output cell, including edge padding, but output-cell clicks only show a generic popup and do not change the computation or display products, and it has no stride control at all.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the key textbook composition: labeled input grid, weight matrix, hidden-layer grid, red convolution lines, highlighted cells, and the same general left-to-right layout. Figure 2 has the same broad elements but is much more flattened and cluttered with many extra zero labels and a formula/control panel, while the diagram labels and proportions are less recognizable compared with the reference.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 is better because it at least includes the key diagram labels from the reference such as “Input, X,” “Weights, Ω,” “Hidden layer, H1,” and the node/weight labels, even though they are quite small at the rendered size. Figure 2 has much heavier label clutter with many invented zero annotations and an extra UI/formula panel not present in the original, while the main figure labels are largely absent or too compressed/illegible, making it less faithful and less readable.

concept.rationale: Both figures miss the brief’s explicit four-panel presentation of successive positions, so neither fully matches the stated structure (L00007). Figure 1 shows the sliding highlighted patch and fixed kernel correctly, but it only implies the multiplication/summation through symbols and lines and gives less direct support for the scalar-output computation, so a student gets a less precise account of the convolution operation than in Figure 2 (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more faithfully preserves the textbook diagram’s geometry, left-to-right composition, labeled input/weights/hidden-layer grids, and recognizable convolution-line layout, whereas Figure 2 reframes the scene into a cluttered isometric/control-panel presentation with less legible or less faithful labels. Figure 2 does outperform Figure 1 on interaction and explicit dot-product feedback, especially with valid stepping, clickable outputs, and stride handling, but those strengths do not outweigh Figure 1’s clearer match to the intended rendered figure and core visual structure.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more consistently reconstructs the pinhole projection geometry: the camera center, image plane, tilted world plane, projected polygon/point, and dashed rays are all placed in mutually consistent 3D positions. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 at least renders a recognizable 3D projection setup with a camera center, camera/image plane, planar surface, dashed projection rays, coordinate axes, cyan point labels, and similar black/gray/cyan/red/green visual coding, even though it is much smaller, cluttered by UI, and less compositionally faithful than the textbook figure. labels.rationale: Figure 1 at least includes several of the original diagram labels such as Camera center, Camera plane, planar surface, coordinate axes, and point annotations, though many are too small and cluttered; Figure 2 fails to render the diagram at all and only shows an error message and reload button, so it has essentially none of the required labels or annotations.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more explicitly and correctly represents the core homography concept: it keeps the world surface as a local Z=0 plane with X,Y,Z axes, places the camera/image plane and rays consistently, and computes/displays a 3x3 homography H from planar world coordinates to image coordinates, matching the collapse from a 3x4 projection to a 3x3 map when all points have form (X,Y,0) (L00007, L00010). aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall result because it actually renders a recognizable pinhole projection scene with camera center, image plane, planar surface, rays, axes, and relevant labels, whereas Figure 2’s rendered output fails with a JavaScript error and therefore provides essentially none of the required visual or labeling content. geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better matches the likely textbook geometry because it reconstructs the camera model and the 2D image-coordinate panel simultaneously as labeled subfigures (a) and (b), with the projection planes placed at ±f along the optical axis, a ray passing through the pinhole, and the 2D panel spatially laid out beside the 3D model. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it reproduces the two-panel structure of the original, including a 3D camera/projection diagram on the left and a boxed camera/image-coordinate diagram on the right with similar labels, colored axes, points, and plane relationships. aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it matches the intended two-panel textbook composition, includes the key annotations and coordinate/image-plane labels, and its authored interactions for dragging P, changing focal length, and toggling virtual/physical projection work more reliably than Figure 1's broken drag handler and inconsistent panel update. faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the main composition of the reference: a left image plane, a right 3D point with red/cyan/green projection geometry, dotted projection ray, and X/Y/Z/f/x/y-style labels in roughly corresponding places. concept.rationale: Both figures correctly place the world point, pinhole, and image point collinearly and use same-colored world/image cross-section triangles to support the proportional relations x/f = X/Z and y/f = Y/Z (L00007, L00010-L00013). Figure 2 is visually closer to the reference and has cleaner, more faithful labels, but relative to Figure 1 it omits important measurement segments and lacks several intended controls, including point dragging and correspondence/side highlighting.
